front: TC005: What is the minimum viable move?
back: Before making any request, answer: what specifically do I need, and by when? State those two things. Leave out the rest.

front: TC005: What is the core sequence?
back: What you need -> By when -> Why it matters -> One ask — stop.

front: TC005: What is the field tip?
back: The kindest request is the clearest one.

front: TC005: What is the strong version of: Vague: 'Could you look at this at some point?'?
back: Can you review section 3 and send your notes by Thursday noon?

front: TC005: What is the strong version of: Over-explaining before making the ask?
back: 'I need your input on X by [date]. Context: one sentence.' Then stop.

front: TC005: What is the strong version of: Multiple bundled requests in one message?
back: One clean request. Then a second message for the next one.

front: TC005: What is better than: 'It would be great if someone could deal with the invoices...'?
back: 'Sam, can you process the invoices by Friday?'

front: TC005: What is better than: 'No rush at all, whenever suits.'?
back: 'Genuinely not urgent — any time before the end of the month.'

front: TC005: What is better than: 'Can you do X, and also Y, and maybe Z if there is time?'?
back: 'The priority is X by Friday. I will come back to the rest separately.'

front: TC005: What are signs it is working?
back: Things get done more often without follow-up chasing. People come back with fewer clarifying questions. You get fewer vague or incomplete responses. You feel clearer about what you need before you ask.

front: TC005: When should you avoid this technique?
back: When the relationship is such that a formal request would feel clinical or cold. In brainstorming contexts where you want open-ended input rather than a specific deliverable.

front: TC005: What is the best recovery line?
back: 'I should have been clearer — what I actually need is X by Y.'
